title: 3-Read Friday #15: Checks for Listening, OneNote, and Paired Coaching
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #15 curates three posts on listening, digital tools, and coaching structure. Jo Castelino, building on Barton's own podcast conversation about "checks for listening," explains how giving students extra time to digest complex information before checking understanding makes those checks more powerful. Adam Boxer makes the case for OneNote as a PowerPoint alternative for classroom teaching, an argument Barton frames against his own recent switch to an iPad-and-Goodnotes setup. Tom Sherrington expands on his podcast comments about favouring group coaching over one-to-one, describing the practicalities of coaching two or three teachers together. Barton frames the set as three practical upgrades to familiar routines: how teachers check understanding, how they present material, and how they coach colleagues.
points: Jo Castelino's technique -- pausing to let students digest complex or multi-step information before checking for listening -- strengthens a check-for-understanding routine Barton discussed on his own podcast.
Adam Boxer's case for OneNote over PowerPoint reflects a broader shift toward tablet-based, live-annotation teaching tools, a switch Barton describes making himself via iPad and Goodnotes.

Tom Sherrington's group-coaching approach coaches two or three teachers together rather than one-to-one, trading some personalisation for shared problem-solving, efficiency, and public commitment to action.
Barton's selections this week are united by a practical, how-to register: each post upgrades a routine (listening checks, lesson materials, coaching structure) that most teachers already use.
quotes: In this lovely post, Jo explains how giving students extra time to digest what they have just heard or seen, especially when it is complex or involves several steps, can make these checks for listening even more powerful and therefore better support understanding.
Inspired by my podcast interview with Pritesh Raichura, I have been building in checks for listening as a bridge between information and checking for understanding.
But Goodnotes is not the only PowerPoint alternative, and in this excellent video, Adam makes a compelling case for using OneNote.
Tom described how he favours group coaching over one-to-one.
When done well, I can see these group sessions being a super positive experience for all involved.
